pages.text: In the nineteenth century, many lands were inhabited by German speakers. People debated how to unite these lands into one nation. This important discussion was known as the German question.
For many years, there was no single country called Germany. Instead, dozens of independent states existed. Leaders wanted to bring these German people together into a single great nation.
Two main ideas developed to solve this problem. The Greater German solution wanted to include all lands with German speakers. The Austrian Empire strongly supported this plan.
The Lesser German solution wanted to unite only the northern states without Austria. The Kingdom of Prussia favored this plan because it would give them strong leadership.
Religion was also an important part of the debate. Catholic regions usually favored Austria, while Protestant northern states preferred Prussia and the House of Hohenzollern.
In eighteen sixty-six, a war changed everything. Prussia defeated Austria, and the lesser German solution won. In eighteen seventy-one, a unified German Empire was finally proclaimed.

B1-B2.headline: Debating German Unification in the 19th Century

pages.text: During the nineteenth century, particularly during the Revolutions of eighteen forty-eight, Europeans debated the German question. This political debate focused on how to achieve the unification of lands inhabited by German speakers.

Political geography showed no single Germany proper. Instead, independent kingdoms, grand duchies, and principalities were ruled by separate sovereigns, though a natural undercurrent pushed toward a national union under one common head.

Two main proposals emerged from this nationalist movement. The Greater German solution favored unifying all German-speaking peoples under Austria, while the Lesser German solution sought to unite northern states under Prussia without Austria.

Religion heavily influenced these allegiances. Catholic regions supported Austria for a dominant Catholic state, whereas Protestant northern states preferred Prussian leadership under the Protestant House of Hohenzollern.

Austria also included many non-German populations, such as Hungarians and Czechs, and was reluctant to abandon those territories. Meanwhile, the Frankfurt Parliament offered the crown to Prussia, but the king rejected it.

The debate ended after Austria suffered a defeat in the eighteen sixty-six Austro-Prussian War. Otto von Bismarck subsequently united the remaining German states under Prussian leadership, successfully establishing the German Empire.

C1-C2.headline: The Geopolitical Evolution of the German Question

pages.text: The nineteenth-century German question encapsulated the complex geopolitical debate regarding the unification of German-inhabited territories. Operating within a confederation of numerous independent states, nationalists sought to resolve the absence of a unified German nation-state.

Centuries of fragmented authority following the decline of the Holy Roman Empire fostered a lasting rivalry between the Austrian Habsburg monarchy and Brandenburg-Prussia, shaping the polarization of nineteenth-century German nationalism.

Proponents of the Großdeutsche Lösung advocated for a Greater Germany incorporating all German-speaking populations under Austrian auspices. Conversely, the Kleindeutsche Lösung promoted a Lesser Germany led exclusively by Prussia, omitting Austrian lands.

Conflicting religious demographics and ethnic diversity complicated these visions. Catholic factions favored Austrian dominance, while Protestant states preferred the Hohenzollern dynasty. Furthermore, Austria's inclusion of substantial non-German populations created significant political friction.

The Revolutions of eighteen forty-eight galvanized these debates through the Frankfurt Parliament, though initial unification attempts faltered when the Prussian monarch rejected the offered imperial crown.

The definitive resolution occurred following Austria's defeat in the eighteen sixty-six Austro-Prussian War. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck leveraged this military outcome to consolidate northern and southern states under Prussian hegemony, culminating in the establishment of the German Empire.
